code: ratings <- calculate_all_ratings(   data = game_data,   initial_rating = 1000,   K = 32,   method = "exponential",   alpha = 1.4,   D = 400 ) # Initial ratings (all start at 1000) current_ratings <- c(Alice = 1000, Bob = 1000, Charlie = 1000, David = 1000)  # Game results game_ranks <- c(Alice = 1, Bob = 2, Charlie = 3, David = NA)  # Update ratings new_ratings <- update_ratings(   game_ranks = game_ranks,   current_ratings = current_ratings,   K = 32,   method = "exponential",   alpha = 1.4 )  # Show changes rating_changes <- new_ratings - current_ratings print("Rating changes:") #> [1] "Rating changes:" head(ratings$ratings_history) #>         date  player    rating game_id #> 1 2024-01-01   Alice 1000.0000       1 #> 2 2024-01-01     Bob 1023.8431       1 #> 3 2024-01-01 Charlie  978.6667       1 #> 4 2024-01-01   David  997.4902       1 #> 5 2024-01-01     Eva 1000.0000       1 #> 6 2024-01-03   Alice  985.0963       2

title: Understanding the Rating System
text: two-player game, player ’s rating updated follows: RAnew=RAold+K×(SA−EA)R_A^{\text{new}} = R_A^{\text{old}} + K \times (S_A - E_A) : RAoldR_A^{\text{old}} player ’s current rating RAnewR_A^{\text{new}} player ’s updated rating KK K-factor (controls rating volatility) SAS_A actual score (1 win, 0 loss, 0.5 draw) EAE_A expected score

title: Understanding the Rating System
text: expected score calculated using logistic function: EA=11+10(RB−RA)/DE_A = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{(R_B - R_A)/D}} : RBR_B opponent’s rating DD scale parameter (typically 400) K D constants can adjusted fine tune behaviour consensus values (e.g., K=32, D=400) work well many scenarios.

title: Understanding the Rating System
text: saw clasical Elo system, games scored follows: - Win = 1 - Draw = 0.5 - Loss = 0 eloextend offers two methods extend multiplayer games: exponential linear. method chosen match intuition much valuable winning compared placing second, third . default exponential scoring α=1.4\alpha = 1.4, think good balance many games.

title: Understanding the Rating System
text: Exponential scoring uses geometric weighting parameter α>0,α≠1\alpha > 0, \alpha \neq 1: si=αN−ri−1∑j=1N(αN−rj−1)s_i = \frac{\alpha^{N - r_i} - 1}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}(\alpha^{N - r_j} - 1)} gives weight top finishers. Higher α\alpha increases disparity ranks, making winning valuable intermediate placements.

title: Understanding the Rating System
text: α\alpha parameter controls much emphasis placed top finishers: α=1.4\alpha = 1.4 (default): Moderate emphasis winners α=2.0\alpha = 2.0: Strong emphasis winners α→1\alpha \1: Approaches linear scoring α→∞\alpha \\infty: Winner-takes-(winner gets score 1, others get 0)  Note 2-player games, exponential scoring formula simplifies : - Winner receives score = 1 - Loser receives score = 0 holds regardless α\alpha, ensuring convergence standard Elo.
code: # Visualise different scoring methods ranks <- 1:5 alphas <- c(1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0)  score_comparison <- data.frame(   rank = ranks,   linear = calculate_scores(ranks, method = "linear") )  for (a in alphas) {   score_comparison[[paste0("exp_", a)]] <- calculate_scores(ranks, method = "exponential", alpha = a) }  score_comparison %>%   pivot_longer(-rank, names_to = "method", values_to = "score") %>%   ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = score, colour = method)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 1) +   geom_point(size = 2) +   labs(     title = "Score Weights by Rank Position",     subtitle = "Including linear and exponential scoring methods",     x = "Rank (1 = winner)",     y = "Normalised Score",     colour = "Method"   ) +   theme_minimal() +   theme(legend.position = "right")

title: Understanding the Rating System
text: scoring methods handle tied ranks assigning equal scores tied players: Bob Charlie receive identical scores despite assigned rank 2.
code: # Two players tied for 2nd place ranks_with_ties <- c(Alice = 1, Bob = 2, Charlie = 2, David = 4)  linear_tied <- calculate_scores(ranks_with_ties, method = "linear") exp_tied <- calculate_scores(ranks_with_ties, method = "exponential", alpha = 1.4)  comparison_tied <- data.frame(   Rank = ranks_with_ties,   Linear = round(linear_tied, 4),   Exponential = round(exp_tied, 4) ) print(comparison_tied) #>         Rank Linear Exponential #> Alice      1   0.50      0.5705 #> Bob        2   0.25      0.2148 #> Charlie    2   0.25      0.2148 #> David      4   0.00      0.0000

title: Understanding the Rating System
text: Linear scoring uses arithmetic weighting based rank position: si=N−ri∑j=1N(N−rj)s_i = \frac{N - r_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}(N - r_j)} rir_i player ii’s rank (1 = best). game without ties, simplifies : si=N−ri(N2)=2(N−ri)N(N−1)s_i = \frac{N - r_i}{\binom{N}{2}} = \frac{2(N - r_i)}{N(N-1)} Linear scoring simpler intuitive exponential, distributing scores evenly across ranks. ’s appropriate games finishing positions matter equally.

title: Understanding the Rating System
text: Linear Scoring: - Simpler - Evenly distributed scores - Good games positions matter equally Exponential Scoring (recommended): - Emphasises winning - closely matches competitive intuitions - Default α=1.4\alpha = 1.4 provides good balance - Tunable behaviour via α\alpha parameter

title: Understanding the Rating System
text: Consider nature game: Low stakes, casual games (α=1.2\alpha = 1.2 1.41.4): friendly Mario Kart nights casual board game groups finishing second third still matters. Competitive games (α=1.4\alpha = 1.4 1.81.8): regular tournaments, ranked online play, competitive board game leagues winning important consistency across finishes matters. Winner-focused games (α=2.0\alpha = 2.0 3.03.0): high-stakes tournaments battle royale-style games winning really counts.

title: Calculate Scores from Rankings — calculate_scores
text: ranks Named numeric vector rankings (1 = best, 2 = second, etc.) Names player identifiers. NA values indicate non-participating players. Tied ranks supported: players rank receive identical scores. method Character string: "linear" "exponential" (default). Linear uses arithmetic weighting, exponential uses geometric weighting. alpha Numeric exponent exponential weighting (used method = "exponential"). Must > 0 != 1. Higher values give weight top finishers. Default 1.4. Note: N=2 players, alpha effect result.

title: Calculate Scores from Rankings — calculate_scores
text: Named numeric vector scores (length names ranks). Non-participating players (NA ranks) receive score 0.

title: Calculate Scores from Rankings — calculate_scores
text: Single-player games (N=1) valid input return score 1 sole participant. However, games meaningless rating updates since competition, update_ratings() modify ratings . 2-player games exponential scoring, formula simplifies give winner score 1 loser score 0, regardless alpha. ensures convergence standard Elo head--head matches. Mathematical explanation: N=2 ranks 1 2, exponential formula gives: Winner (rank 1): (alpha^(2-1) - 1) / ((alpha^(2-1) - 1) + (alpha^(2-2) - 1)) = (alpha - 1) / (alpha - 1 + 0) = 1 Loser (rank 2):  (alpha^(2-2) - 1) / ((alpha^(2-1) - 1) + (alpha^(2-2) - 1)) = 0 / (alpha - 1) = 0 Thus, alpha cancels 2-player case.

code: # Simple ranking without NAs calculate_scores(c(Alice = 1, Bob = 2, Charlie = 3, David = 4), method = "linear") #>     Alice       Bob   Charlie     David  #> 0.5000000 0.3333333 0.1666667 0.0000000  calculate_scores(c(Alice = 1, Bob = 2, Charlie = 3, David = 4),                  method = "exponential", alpha = 1.4) #>     Alice       Bob   Charlie     David  #> 0.5618557 0.3092784 0.1288660 0.0000000   # With non-participating players (NAs) ranks <- c(Alice = 1, Bob = 3, Charlie = 2, David = NA) calculate_scores(ranks, method = "exponential", alpha = 1.4) #>     Alice       Bob   Charlie     David  #> 0.7058824 0.0000000 0.2941176 0.0000000   # With tied ranks (tied players receive equal scores) calculate_scores(c(Alice = 1, Bob = 2, Charlie = 2, David = 4), method = "linear") #>   Alice     Bob Charlie   David  #>    0.50    0.25    0.25    0.00   # For 2 players with exponential, alpha doesn't matter: calculate_scores(c(Alice = 1, Bob = 2), method = "exponential", alpha = 1.4) #> Alice   Bob  #>     1     0  calculate_scores(c(Alice = 1, Bob = 2), method = "exponential", alpha = 10) #> Alice   Bob  #>     1     0
